newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour returns to VAT attack on Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour returns to VAT attack on Conservatives.

text.p: The opposition Labour party accused the Conservative party on Monday of issuing "post-dated" cheques for spending commitments to be financed after the election, now less than four months away.

As Prime Minister John Major discussed the contents of the ruling party's manifesto with his cabinet at his official country retreat, Labour repeated charges that the Conservatives were planning to put Value Added Tax on food.
"It is only two months since the budget, but already the Tories (Conservatives) have made a series of spending commitments which were not covered in the budget plans...
"How will they raise the extra money?" Labour Deputy Leader John Prescott asked a news conference.

"We will remind people that whatever they say before an election, the Tories cannot be trusted, especially on VAT. They told us they would cut taxes year on year and then they gave us the biggest tax increases in peacetime history."
Labour's trade spokeswoman Margaret Beckett unveiled a survey by the NOP polling organisation showing 53 percent of voters believed it was likely the Conservatives would introduce VAT on food.
Beckett added: "This fear will be reinforced by the way that in the run-up to the election the Tories seem determined to issue one post-dated cheque after another...

"There has been the commitment to pay for the Royal Yacht to the tune of some 60 million pounds ($97.39 million) and the pledge to extend the cadet force which has been costed at a potential 1.5 billion pounds."
Defence Secretary Michael Portillo announced last week the government would pay for a new Royal Yacht out of public funds in a move he apparently thought would boost the ruling party's image.
But the advantage began to fray after Labour, which has a 20 point poll lead, said it would not finance a new yacht when health and education badly needed public funds.
Labour accused Major of failing to consult other parties and former Conservative Prime Minister Edward Heath said the decision should have been delayed until after the election.
"The Conservative Party above all must be an honourable party. And I don't believe the actions that have been taken are honourable ones," Heath told BBC radio.
